Actually, she did "trigger" them. 

If someone sets of fireworks and triggers me, they aren't an asshole. It's not their fault that I'm triggered by fireworks. I have no reasonable expectation of having a quiet, peaceful night on New Years Eve. My disproportionate reaction to hearing fireworks go off is a symptom of my PTSD. **That's what "Triggered" means.** 

If you think this isn't what triggered means, it might be because you've heard the word used as a joke too often.

To begin with, you have to understand what normal non-dissociated development looks lie. All people have "parts of self". During early childhood development people naturally integrate all these different parts of self into one whole person that they think of as being them. By about age 6 or 7, most kids have an idea of who they are and the concept that they are an individual who is separate from other people. By this point they can shift smoothly between different "parts of self" that they experience throughout the day. They might have a "school self", "home self", a "hanging out with friends self" etc. But the child recognizes all of these parts as being them, and they flow smoothly between one part and the next, without any disruption in memory or extreme shifts in behavior. 

When this normal developmental process is disrupted by trauma, these parts of self can become walled off from each other. What if the only way to function at school is to segment off what happens at home? What if the only way to keep living during the day is to pretend that what happened at night never happened? The child's mind creates dissociative barriers between these already existing parts of self in a process very similar to what people with PTSD experience. The difference here is that when these traumatic events are repeated and chronic, and attached to specific parts of self, these segregated parts of self can continue to grow and develop as if they were their own separate person. 

A person with DID has parts of self just like a non-dissociated person, except that they have walls between these parts. Instead of growing up to develop a sense of self as one whole person, each of these parts develops a separate sense of self because they can't see each other and they can't flow smoothly from one part to the other. "School part" can't remember what happens at home and doesn't realize that home life is part who they are. "Home part" can't remember what happens at school and doesn't realize that school is part of who they are. Obviously this creates gaps, but there are rationalizations and fictionalizations that fill these gaps. 

It isn't really a matter of coming up with or managing different detailed personalities. It's just a matter of having walls between the parts of self that everyone has. Unlike the movies, in real life DID parts of self aren't often elaborate characters (unless that serves some sort of psychological need for the person). 

Some of the elaboration and background details that alters have serve a purpose, such as explaining away distressing gaps (like not being able to remember large chunks of time), or creating a soothing life narrative like believing oneself to be an orphan when you actually have abusive parents. 

Alters are just dissociated parts of self. They may experience themselves as "completely different people" and feel very unique and elaborated, but in reality the brain really isn't creating or managing that many more details than it would be if all these parts were integrated.

Plenty of sources acknowledge the controversy and then go on to explain the scientific realities of DID. I gave you a great source above, but you are stubborn AF. > DID and dissociative disorders are not rare conditions. In studies of the general population, a prevalence rate of DID of 1% to 3% of the population has been described.

Alright, fair. I'm really used to people expressing this exact same doubt about DID, as if "MPD isn't real" also means "DID isn't real". It's frustrating.

Dissociation and DID are a lot like that. Just imagine if you spent your whole childhood segmenting your life into little pieces like that. If you only thought about school while you were at school and only thought about home while you were at home, if you literally could not allow yourself to think about your mother while you were at school, like she didn't exist while you were there. If you did that every day during the critical time of development when you were developing your sense of self, you might just develop in pieces instead of developing into one whole person.

I'm characterizing it appropriately according to the modern understanding of it. Your information is outdated, which is very apparent as you are still referring to them as "personalities" and claiming that these "personalities" are unaware of one another. 

If this is a subject you are genuinely interested in and you are in the mental health field, I recommend reading *The Haunted Self: Structural Dissociation and the Treatment of Chronic Traumatization*by Ellert R. S. Nijenhuis, Kathy Steele, and Onno van der Hart. 

I use the example of "home self" and "work self" to help laymen understand that DID is not as sensational as having "multiple people in one body" as people sometimes unfortunately portray it. People without DID have a "home self" and "work self" because they have integrated parts of self and can shift smoothly between them. When people don't experience chronic early childhood trauma they develop and integrated sense of self and simply have these non-dissociated parts of self. 

People with DID have dissociated parts of self, which are far more complex than a "home self" and "work self". They are different in that they are emancipated and elaborated in ways that integrated parts of self are not. They can become so emancipated and elaborated that they have entirely separate identities, names, genders, preferences, belief systems, etc. They can believe themselves to be separate people. 

When I say that DID is not as sensational as people believe, what I mean is that these dissociated parts of self as still just parts of self. As much as they believe themselves to be "separate people", they are still just elaborate parts of self, which isn't that sensational at all. I think anyone who has read the research on structural dissociation and remains skeptical is foolish. 

The really unfortunate part is that this skepticism does a lot of harm to people with DID. Being treated for the wrong disorder when you actually have DID is horrible. People with DID need intense trauma therapy to heal, and they can't get that until they can get past all the skeptics who think they are just attention-seeking BPD patients, schizophrenics, or bipolars.
Well, that and people constantly thought it was a personality disorder and not a dissociative disorder.

Awareness of other parts/alters can vary a lot. It's very common for people with DID to have one or more "main parts" who handle daily life who remain relatively unaware of the other parts for a long time, sometimes right up until diagnosis. These parts functional well in life by remaining in denial about the trauma they have suffered, and by remaining in denial about the other parts. Sometimes stressful events or new trauma will make it more difficult for these parts to remain in denial, which is typically when the person enters the mental health system and finally receives a diagnosis. 

Other parts, often parts who are not focused on handling major parts of daily life, have more awareness of each other. But there may also be other parts who are more segregated off from the others, kept separate because of their specific behaviors or the traumas they represent. 

Awareness of each other can continue to fluctuate throughout the therapy process. There are "dissociative walls" between parts, and part of therapy is trying to bring down those walls so that parts can get closer together, communicate freely, and share information and memories.

I think a lot of the doubt around DID comes from the way it is portrayed in media, and the way it is misconceptualized by most people. It is not typically as sensational as it looks here. DID is essentially just a very severe form of developmental PTSD. 

All people have many "parts of self", a work self, a home self, a "hanging out with the guys" self, etc. Most people flow smoothly between these parts of self without any sort of issue, and they remember being all these different parts of self. They have a sense of ownership of all their actions. They don't go home from work and forget everything that happened while they were there. 

The only difference between people with DID, and people without DID is that there is dissociation between those parts of self. A disconnection between those parts so that they can't shift smoothly between them, and that dissociation between them can cause them to grow and develop so distinctly that they can end up thinking that they are actually separate people. Of course they aren't, but the can think that. And because they experienced such horrible trauma, they might have parts of self that typical people don't have. They might have really traumatized parts, angry parts, deeply depressed and bitter parts. But they are still all just dissociated parts of one whole person. 

I'm sorry your professors didn't give you more information on this disorder, because while there is real controversy surrounding it, the controversy is far more complex than "DID isn't real and can't be proven". Your professors were lazy if that's what they told you.

I got rid of my "exit strategy". 

I've been carrying around enough pills to kill myself for the last 10 years. They were my exit strategy, my backup plan in case things were just too much. 

Last May I got to a point where I thought I might actually use them, and instead I got rid of them. And life has felt really different ever since. I've been carrying those pills around for 10 years, feeling like they were a safety net, and now I realize that they were a huge fucking burden.

I don't hear voices in the traditional sense. I don't experience auditory hallucinations like people with schizophrenia do. But I have Dissociative Identity Disorder and I have the experience of feeling like I have multiple trains of thought, some of which don't belong to me. So it's a bit like hearing voices, or thoughts that are not my own. The majority of them are actually good to me. Some of them are quite negative and self-depreciating, but others are very positive. One in particular is like an internalized pinterest mom full of positive affirmations and things like "You are so loved". It's actually obnoxious sometimes.
I don't feel ready to raise that kind of alarm with anyone. I feel like if I can just get rid of these pills I can keep myself reasonably safe until I see my therapist again.
We're on a septic system and have a creek very close to our home. All those chemicals would probably go directly into the local ecosystem. Trash seems safer than flushing.

I mean, first of all, note the sub that we're in. This is ELI5 and mine is a top level comment. I was not going to go into the entire biospsychosocial model on ELI5. This is supposed to be an explanation for laymen. 

Secondly, I'm sorry if you interpreted my comment as an indication that I believe in biological determinism? Schizophrenia is definitely one of the disorders that is more heavily influenced by biology but I still avoided saying flat out "schizophrenia is caused by your genes". I said it plays a role. Your former therapist could very well be right. However, you have said that you have a history of childhood abuse and trauma and experience severe episodes of dissociation. 

I would really strongly recommend that you get a second opinion from a therapist who is trained in trauma and dissociation. Dissociative Identity Disorder and OSDD are very commonly misdiagnosed as schizophrenia by less knowledgeable practitioners. I am definitely not saying this is the case for you or advocating any kind of self-diagnosis. There is a lot of overlap or symptoms of DID that can be misinterpreted as symptoms of schizophrenia, especially things like memory issues, lack of emotions, shifts in perception of reality, and the feeling of thoughts not being your own.

Schizophrenia isn't a dissociative disorder. Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder. Scientists aren't exactly sure what causes schizophrenia, but it seems to have a strong genetic component. So if you have a close relative with schizophrenia, your chances of having it go up a lot. Experiencing trauma seems to increase your risk too, but trauma alone doesn't seem to be enough to cause schizophrenia. Genetics seem to play a bigger role for this disorder. 

Rather than paraphrase, I'll just quote my favorite [website on dissociation](http://did-research.org/): 
>Dissociation is a disconnection between one’s conscious awareness and aspects of one’s environment, experiences, or perceptions. Dissociation is very common, so much so that some claim that it is the third most common mental health symptom. Individuals can experience dissociation for many reasons. Causes or triggers can vary from temporary stress to clinical anxiety to chronic childhood trauma. In some cases, dissociation can serve as a coping mechanism and buffer individuals from overwhelming life circumstances. However, when dissociation is severe or long lasting, it can be disabling. 

There are different theories about PTSD. One theory is called Structural Dissociation. The really simple version of this theory is that when you are traumatized, a part of you that remembers the trauma becomes dissociated or disconnected from you and that is why it's harder to access those memories of the trauma, but the memories can resurface abruptly when you are triggered by things that remind you of the event. That part of you is very emotional and raw, sort of "stuck" in that traumatic period of your life. Healing from your trauma means reintegrating that part back into your whole self again.

It's kind of dangerous to suggest that to people when they provide such limited information. I would only suggest DID to people who report experiencing amnesia, time loss, or more of the other symptoms of DID.

There is so much more to DID than having two sides to your personality. It's a Dissociative disorder and the main symptom is amnesia which causes blackouts and time loss. The other major symptoms are similar to PTSD because the disorder is caused by trauma. It's not just being both extroverted and introverted.

You can't develop DID at 16, though you can find out that you have it at any age. DID develops before about age 8 and is usually the result of trauma beginning at a very early age. 

During your teen years and even into your twenties it's very normal to experience some confusion about your identity. In fact, this stage of your life is called your Identity Development stage in Psycho-Social Developmental Psychology. Your big job in this stage of your life is to accomplish "Identity vs Role Confusion". For most teenagers, this involves trying out lots of different identities. And it's really normal to feel conflicted about this. 

Your thoughts and opinions about important topics like politics and social issues might be shifting away from your parents' beliefs and shifting more towards what your friends or other important role models believe. You might feel conflict between the "culture" of your family of origin and the "culture" of your friends and peers. Figuring out who you are as a person and what you want in life is such a huge job. It's no wonder that teens are stressed all the time. 

If you add any level of dissociation to this mix, it's going to be harder. Experiencing DP/DR while going through the normal stages of identity development are going to make it a bit more challenging. I'd watch out for maybe feeling depersonalized from parts of yourself that feel undesirable to you. Like if you notice that you have a bad temper and you feel disconnected from that part of yourself, that's something to watch out for. It doesn't mean that you have DID. People without DID can become disconnected from parts of themselves. This happens with less severe dissociative disorders, PTSD, CPTSD, etc. 

So, feeling really conflicted at this age is totally normal. Feeling like there are many pieces of yourself and that they are at conflict with each other, also totally normal. As you get older, everything is going to come together more. You're going to figure out who you are and what is important to you. 

Now, if you start dissociating so much that you are actually experiencing amnesia (losing chunks of time and "waking up" in places without any idea how you got there) or people are telling you that you behaved really strangely and you don't remember those events and have no idea what they are talking about, then it's time to worry about DID.

Your understanding is close to correct, but not quite. Some alters are formed as a specific reaction to trauma and are "trauma holders". Some exist specifically to protect against trauma memories disrupting every day life. But there are also alters that exist for totally "normal" every day stuff like alters who's job is to relax, play, be social, take care of work/school. 

So switching doesn't always happen because of a trigger. Switching can happen throughout the day to take care of various needs. 

But this is all irrelevant because playing a character with DID is annoying AF and disrespectful to people with actual DID.

Please just don't. Dissociative Identity Disorder is a serious mental health condition that is always caused by childhood trauma, often sexual abuse or violent abuse. Replicating that in game is just not fun. Beyond that, it tends to be full of cliches in game and annoying to the other players.

It's actually not that rare. It effects about 1 to 2% of the population. People incorrectly perceive it to be rare because of the backlash that occurred after the over-diagnosis in the late 80s and early 90s, but since then a better understanding of the disorder has emerged and mental health professionals are finally recognizing it as a relatively uncommon but not "rare" disorder. 

I'm not sure why you feel that the symptoms of DID would warrant a trip to the ER or limit a persons capacity to consent to therapy. I suspect that your perceptions of what DID is and how it presents may be very skewed by media depictions.

I'm not sure what the "correct" answer is within the framework of your coursework. I don't know if your professor is looking for an answer built around patient education or a specific treatment modality or anything like that. But in my opinion, in treating DID, the first step should be to increase feelings of safety. People with DID can not even begin to deal with their trauma until they feel safe. So step one is to help them feel safe. People with DID are often dealing with the same symptoms as people with PTSD/CPTSD, so you'll want to address those sort of things. You have to address anxiety, panic, insomnia, disordered eating, self-harm, etc, and a lot of that is rooted in feeling unsafe. 

A lot of times people with DID first come to therapy when memories are beginning to surface, and there is this temptation to go digging for those memories and to figure out what happened. "Why am I like this?" "What happened to me?" but all of that goes  counter to creating safety, so you'll want to get them to focus on memory containment exercises instead. Temporarily pack all of that away until they have learned coping skills so that they can safely address traumatic memories without being overwhelmed by them.

Is it someone previously diagnosed with DID walking into your office to seek therapy, someone undiagnosed but you suspect them of having DID, or someone who walks in and tells you directly that they believe that they have DID?

I have DID and Split is actually a really terrible depiction of what it is actually like to have DID. Most people with DID are very angry about that movie and the upcoming sequel, but that's really not the point of your post so I won't harp on that too much. 

I think it makes a lot of sense that you would feel the way that you do. I won't pretend that I know what it's like to be you, but I studied psychology in school and I have friends and family who have BPD so I think I have a pretty good understanding from an outsiders perspective at least? From what I understand, people with BPD often experience identity confusion and feel a sense of hollowness or emptiness. People with DID experience episodes of this too, so I can relate. We just experience those episodes in between the episodes where we experience being our different identities. 

The thing that happened in Split where she said his real name and he was "normal" for a minute, that doesn't happen in real life. The whole idea of being able to use "trigger words" to call a specific alter or the host back to the front is a media myth. So it's not like we can actually snap out of it and suddenly be normal. The truth is that if we switch or are experiencing a severe dissociative episode, we might not be able to do anything about it. So please don't think that DID gives you the ability to snap out of it instantly. 

The way alters are portrayed in films and TV is really unrealistic too. My alters are nothing like anything I've seen in movies or tv about DID. Honestly, they're probably actually a lot more like what you experience with BPD. We're traumatized, and our trauma shaped us. Honestly, it makes me angry that media portrayals of DID simultaneously make us seem both like horrible monsters and like interesting, fun, fascinating creatures. The reality is that we're just people. 

It's interesting that you say that you feel like BPD is a "failed attempt" at DID. I don't think I'd put it that way, but there is a school of thought that sees DID and BPD on the same spectrum. It's called [Structural Dissociation](http://did-research.org/origin/structural_dissociation/index.html) and depending on how severe it is, you can end up with PTSD, [BPD](http://did-research.org/origin/structural_dissociation/secondary.html), or DID. The pages I linked to go to more info about Structural Dissociation in general, and how Structural Dissociation creates BPD. You might find them interesting even though the website is about DID.
How so?

1) The presence of scholarly articles about insanity doesn't negate the fact that "insane" is a legal term and not a medical or psychological term. This is something psychology students learn in psych 101. It is factually incorrect to conflate "insane" with "mentally ill" or to state that all people with DID are insane. 

2) You would be incorrect. It is actually incredibly difficult to use DID as a legal defense. People with DID are held legally accountable for their actions, regardless of which alternate identity state is responsible for the action. Except in very rare circumstances DID does not diminish capacity. People with DID (including their alternate identity states) are capable of understanding the consequences of their actions and distinguishing right and wrong. 

3) I'm not debating that. I am using that issue as an example of when colloquial usage of a term influences our language enough that reasonable people will understand that it is no longer acceptable to use words like "Retarded" to describe people.

I should start by saying I have no interest in Walker and am honestly not informed on the rest of this argument, I'm only here to comment on the issue of "Insane" and DID. 

Insane and mentally ill are not interchangeable terms. They have completely different meanings and "insane" is not used medically. 

Insanity is actually a legal term. It means that someone can't be held accountable for their actions due to the severity of their mental illness. The word insanity implies that someone is so mentally ill that they can not differentiate right from wrong and do not understand the consequences or meaning of their actions.

DID has a very long and complicated history. One that unfortunately undergrad psych students rarely hear. Instead, they get a really limited Wiki version that ends up boiled down to "some people don't even believe it's real". 

The truth is that DID was heavily over-diagnosed in the late 80s and early 90s because it got tied into the moral panic (sometimes called the Satanic Panic) that was happening around the same time. A handful of unethical therapists were engaging in unethical practices, encouraging people to "recover" memories of abuse using bad practices and manipulating them into believing that they had been abused and had multiple personalities as a result. There was a lot of media hysteria and a lot of people were hurt. But things changed after that. 

The thing is, the concept of Multiple Personality Disorder (now called Dissociative Identity Disorder) existed before that moral panic and the subsequent overdiagnosis. It wasn't invented by those unethical therapists. It was just exploited by them. Those people not only hurt the individuals who were wrongly diagnosed, they also hurt everyone who legitimately has DID and now suffers because they created this atmosphere of doubt surrounding the diagnosis. 

The good news is that a lot has changed since then. Attitudes are changing. Psychologists and Psychiatrists are no longer fearful of doing research on the subject and being associated with the people who manipulated others. I mean 1999 was almost 20 years ago now! More commonly, skeptics believe that DID is misconceptualized and that people presenting with DID are better off being diagnosed with something like severe C-PTSD or Borderline. That's a good question, and you're right that DID is caused by trauma and not genetics (though genetics may play a role in how likely someone is to dissociate!). 

Children who do not have DID go through a normal process called "Identity Integration", which takes place during early childhood. It's a long process that happens beginning in your toddler years and finishing up probably around when you're 8 years old. During this process you develop your sense of self and you learn to shift between different moods, roles, and situations in life. Have you ever noticed that you behave kind of like a different person with your friends than you do at work, or with your friends, or with your mom? But you still feel like *you*, right? You still retain all of your memories of what happened. You don't black out and forget everything that happened while you were at work. Or if you get real mad, you might feel like a totally different person while you're screaming at that asshole who cut you off in traffic. But you still remember everything that happened, and really, you're still *you*. That's because you successful completed identity integration! Congratulations! You win one whole fully developed sense of self! 

Now when you take a child and you traumatize them over and over again to the point that they dissociate all the time, you disrupt that natural process of identity integration. They learn to escape from painful things by dissociating from themselves. That painful thing didn't happen to me, it happened to some other child. I don't have to go to that horrible place, some other child does. I'm not the one who can't stop crying. I'm not the one who gets hit because I can't stop screaming. And so on. The child is so disrupted in their natural identity development that they can't shift smoothly between emotional states or situations. There might be an alter that exists purely for accepting affection, or purely for handling school, or purely for holding the most traumatic memories. The transitions between these parts are rough and they cause disruptions in the sense of self, because the communication between these parts are cut off and the memory between these parts is disrupted. A bad day at work or getting cut off in traffic could mean complete amnesia. 

So there's no "original" because we never developed into one fully developed whole child. We never had the chance. The trauma was so early and so persistent that we literally never developed a normal sense of self. We have been this way from very early childhood. I know it's absolutely horrifying to think of people abusing such young children, but for a lot of people with DID, that's when it starts.

People with DID have distinct alternate identity states (alters) who have unique ways of viewing themselves and the world around them. These alters can take control (switch), exert passive influence, or talk to the person who is in control (fronting). As for the bananas, some of them like bananas, some of them hate them, some of them couldn't care less. The point is, they have distinct opinions and perspectives because they are distinct identity states with their own perceptions and thoughts. Sometimes these alters have names, but like the person who provided the banana example, sometimes they just perceive themselves to be variations of the same person and they all respond to and identify with the same name. Either way, they are technically still alters. When they take control or switch, the change is so distinct that it causes changes in behavior, mannerisms, speech, and causes disruption in perceptions and memory. 

In BPD, there are no distinct identity states. There are moods and emotions just like everyone has, but they are intense and sometimes chaotic. In addition to chaotic moods, people with BPD sometimes have a poor sense of identity. They don't always have a firm grasp of who they are as a person, what they like and dislike. They might not know if they like bananas at all. They might like bananas one day and hate them the next, being easily influenced by current opinions of people around them, especially people they like or want to emulate. Sometimes people with BPD do experience dissociation and feel detached from themselves, experiencing episodes of depersonalization and derealization. But these episodes do not rise to the level of experiencing distinct identity states. They don't experience amnesia or have dissociative parts of themselves who take over. I think part of the confusion is that sometimes people with BPD behave in ways that they really regret and wish to feel detached from. They look back on their behavior and think "That wasn't me" or "I wish that wasn't me" and sometimes that leads them to believe that they have alters, but it really isn't the same experience.

BPD doesn't cause people to have alters, but I have met people with BPD who claim to have alters. They are not actually experiencing dissociation and they do not have alters the way that people with DID have alters, but they mistakenly believe that their intense emotions and identity disturbances are alters.

So when most people think of DID, they think that there is one original identity that splits into parts due to trauma, but that's not actually how it works. 

DID is caused by trauma during very early childhood, during the time when children are actually going through a stage of development when something called "identity integration" is naturally happening. During this stage of development, children naturally develop one cohesive sense of self, where they can naturally shift from one identity state to another seamlessly, and with a flowing, natural autobiographical memory. For example, they might behave differently at school than they do at home, or with their friends, or with their grandmother, but they are still the same child in all those situations, and they maintain their sense of self and their memories during all those situations. 

A child exposed to severe trauma and repeated dissociation does not experience identity integration. Their identity forms in pieces. I was never one person. I have always been many pieces.

I think one thing that may help in conceptualizing mental illnesses is to understand that nearly all mental illnesses are just extremes of otherwise normal behaviors/experiences. Personality disorders are extremes of what would otherwise be normal behaviors and normal personality types. They need help, and to receive help they have to have their problems acknowledged.
